claim: The EEG spectral composition of NREMS in healthy mice shows an infraslow (~50 s) interval over which microarousals appear preferentially.
source: We found that the EEG spectral composition of non-rapid eye movement sleep (NREMS) in healthy mice shows an infraslow (~50 s) interval over which microarousals appear preferentially.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1 showing the timing relationship between microarousals and the 0.02 Hz-fluctuation in sigma power.

claim: In the spared nerve injury (SNI) mouse model of chronic neuropathic pain, there are more numerous local cortical arousals accompanied by heart rate increases in hindlimb primary somatosensory cortex.
source: In the spared nerve injury (SNI) mouse model of chronic neuropathic pain, we found more numerous local cortical arousals accompanied by heart rate increases in hindlimb primary somatosensory, but not in prelimbic, cortices, although sleep macroarchitecture appeared unaltered.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figures 5 and 6 showing increased activation indices and heart rate changes in S1HL but not PrL cortex.

claim: Sleep macroarchitecture appeared unaltered in the SNI mouse model of chronic neuropathic pain.
source: In the spared nerve injury (SNI) mouse model of chronic neuropathic pain, we found more numerous local cortical arousals accompanied by heart rate increases in hindlimb primary somatosensory, but not in prelimbic, cortices, although sleep macroarchitecture appeared unaltered.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 3 showing no significant differences in sleep time, bout lengths, or microarousal frequency between Sham and SNI groups.

claim: Closed-loop mechanovibrational stimulation revealed higher sensory arousability in SNI mice.
source: Closed-loop mechanovibrational stimulation further revealed higher sensory arousability.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 8 showing increased wake-up probability in response to vibration stimuli in SNI mice compared to Sham controls.

claim: Chronic pain preserved conventional sleep measures but resulted in elevated spontaneous and evoked arousability.
source: Chronic pain thus preserved conventional sleep measures but resulted in elevated spontaneous and evoked arousability.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing normal sleep architecture (Figure 3) but increased local cortical arousals (Figure 6) and higher sensory arousability (Figure 8).

claim: Microarousals in mice are defined as ≤16 s awakenings accompanied by movement activity seen in the EMG.
source: Undisturbed NREMS was frequently interrupted by brief arousal events that are called microarousals (MAs), defined in mouse as ≤16 s awakenings accompanied by movement activity seen in the EMG (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim cites Franken et al., 1999 as the source for this definition and is supported by the methodology described in the manuscript.

claim: The onset of microarousals coincided with declining or low sigma power levels that followed a pronounced sigma power peak.
source: The onset of MAs coincided with declining or low sigma power levels that followed a pronounced sigma power peak (Figure 1B and C), which is characteristic for a fragility period in which sensory arousability is high (Lecci et al., 2017; Fernandez and Lüthi, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and C and cites previous work by Lecci et al., 2017 and Fernandez and Lüthi, 2020.

claim: The mean preferred phase of microarousal onset was 151.6° ± 1.1°, with 180° representing the sigma power trough.
source: The phase values of the 0.02 Hz-fluctuation, calculated via a Hilbert transform (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), showed that MA onset times clustered around a mean preferred phase of 151.6° ± 1.1°, with 180° representing the sigma power trough (Rayleigh test, p<1 × 10–16).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Rayleigh test) of phase values from 9476 microarousals in 30 mice.

claim: The majority of microarousals (89%) were clustered between 90 and 270° of the 0.02 Hz-fluctuation phase.
source: The majority of MAs (89%) were clustered between 90 and 270°, which narrows the fragility period to the low values of sigma power around the trough (Lecci et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by phase analysis data and cites Lecci et al., 2017.

claim: The phase locking of microarousals to the 0.02 Hz-fluctuation was observed when time points at 4, 8, and 12 s before the onset of a microarousal were quantified.
source: The phase locking was also observed when time points at 4, 8, and 12 s before the onset of an MA were quantified (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The onset of the fragility period preceded the microarousal.
source: This shows that the onset of the fragility period preceded the MA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the phase locking data showing clustering at time points before microarousal onset.

claim: Fragility periods constitute moments during which microarousals preferentially occur.
source: Fragility periods thus constitute moments during which MAs preferentially occur.
evidence: The claim is supported by the phase clustering data showing preferential occurrence of microarousals during specific phases of the 0.02 Hz-fluctuation.

claim: The phase relations between microarousals and the 0.02 Hz-fluctuation persisted for all 1-hr intervals across time of day.
source: These phase relations persisted for all 1-hr intervals across time of day (Figure 1E), although the density of MAs showed a characteristic increase towards the end of the light phase and was higher during the dark phase (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: The density of microarousals showed a characteristic increase towards the end of the light phase and was higher during the dark phase.
source: These phase relations persisted for all 1-hr intervals across time of day (Figure 1E), although the density of MAs showed a characteristic increase towards the end of the light phase and was higher during the dark phase (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The peak frequency of the 0.02 Hz-fluctuation remained relatively constant, with a minor decrease in power during the dark phase.
source: The peak frequency of the 0.02 Hz-fluctuation also remained relatively constant, with a minor decrease in power during the dark phase (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Across the 24 hr cycle, a median of 33.6% of all fragility periods was accompanied by a microarousal.
source: Across the 24 hr cycle, a median of 33.6% of all fragility periods was accompanied by an MA (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Microarousals appeared predominantly during fragility periods, while a majority of fragility periods occurred with NREMS remaining consolidated.
source: This means that MAs appeared predominantly during fragility periods, while a majority of fragility periods occurred with NREMS remaining consolidated.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that 33.6% of fragility periods contained microarousals, meaning the majority did not.

claim: Power spectral analysis of SNI animals in quiet wakefulness showed power elevations starting at frequencies around 5 Hz for S1HL.
source: Indeed, power spectral analysis of animals with SNI in quiet but not active wakefulness showed power elevations starting at frequencies around 5 Hz-for S1HL (Figure 2D and E, left), leading to increased relative power within the theta (5–10 Hz), beta (16–25 Hz) and the low gamma (26–40 Hz) ranges (Figure 2E, right, mixed-model ANOVA for 'treatment' × 'frequency band,' p=2.08 × 10–4, post-hoc t-test for SNI vs. Sham, for theta, p=0.004, for beta, p=0.006, for low gamma, p=0.006, with Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.008).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of power spectral data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SNI animals showed increased relative power within the theta (5–10 Hz), beta (16–25 Hz) and the low gamma (26–40 Hz) ranges in S1HL during quiet wakefulness.
source: Indeed, power spectral analysis of animals with SNI in quiet but not active wakefulness showed power elevations starting at frequencies around 5 Hz-for S1HL (Figure 2D and E, left), leading to increased relative power within the theta (5–10 Hz), beta (16–25 Hz) and the low gamma (26–40 Hz) ranges (Figure 2E, right, mixed-model ANOVA for 'treatment' × 'frequency band,' p=2.08 × 10–4, post-hoc t-test for SNI vs. Sham, for theta, p=0.004, for beta, p=0.006, for low gamma, p=0.006, with Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.008).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (mixed-model ANOVA and post-hoc t-tests) of power spectral data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Analysis of PrL indicated a significant increase in the theta band in SNI animals during quiet wakefulness.
source: Similar analyses for PrL indicated a significant increase in the theta band (Figure 2F and G, mixed-model ANOVA for G, 'treatment' × 'frequency band,' p=0.008, post-hoc t-test for SNI vs. Sham, for theta, p=0.007, with Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.008).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (mixed-model ANOVA and post-hoc t-test) of power spectral data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The peripheral nerve injury led to alterations in brain activity that have been described previously as signatures of pain.
source: We hence concluded that the peripheral nerve injury led to alterations in brain activity that have been described previously as signatures of pain (LeBlanc et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim cites LeBlanc et al., 2014 and is supported by the power spectral analysis data showing increased theta and gamma power.

claim: SNI and Sham controls spent similar amounts of time asleep in the 12 hr light and dark phases at both baseline and D20+.
source: Based on these data, SNI and Sham controls spent similar amounts of time asleep in the 12 hr light and dark phases, during both baseline and at D20+ (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Both SNI and Sham treatment groups showed minor increases (2.4–3%) in NREMS time at the expense of wakefulness at D20+ compared to baseline in both light and dark phases.
source: Both treatment groups showed minor increases (2.4–3%) in NREMS time at the expense of wakefulness at D20+ compared to baseline in both light and dark phases (mixed-model ANOVAs with factors 'treatment' and 'day,' p=0.0013 in light phase, p=8.5 × 10–6 in dark phase for 'day,' p>0.8 for 'treatment' for either light or dark phase, no interaction).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (mixed-model ANOVAs) of sleep time data.

claim: Cumulative distributions of NREMS and REMS bout lengths at D20+ were similar for Sham and SNI, with only a minor shift toward smaller values in SNI.
source: Moreover, cumulative distributions of NREMS and REMS bout lengths at D20+ were similar for Sham and SNI, with only a minor shift toward smaller values in SNI for both NREMS (Figure 3B, –2.3 s; Kolmogorov–Smirnov [KS] test, p=0.015) and REMS (–3 s; KS test, p=0.026).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests) of bout length distributions shown in Figure 3B.

claim: When subdivided into short, intermediate, and long bouts for the light phase, there were no significant differences between Sham and SNI for both NREMS and REMS.
source: When subdivided into short, intermediate, and long bouts for the light phase, there were no significant differences between Sham and SNI for both NREMS and REMS (Figure 3B, mixed-model ANOVAs for 'treatment' × 'bout length,' p=0.79 for NREMS, p=0.23 for REMS).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (mixed-model ANOVAs) of bout length data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Sleep onset latency was not altered by treatment or time post-surgery.
source: Furthermore, sleep onset latency (Figure 3C) and NREMS fragmentation by MAs (Figure 3D; Franken et al., 1999), were not altered by treatment or time post-surgery (mixed-model ANOVA with factors 'treatment' and 'day,' for sleep onset latency, p=0.42 and p=0.94, no interactions; for number of MAs, p=0.79 and p=0.43, no interactions).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (mixed-model ANOVAs) of sleep onset latency data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: NREMS fragmentation by microarousals was not altered by treatment or time post-surgery.
source: Furthermore, sleep onset latency (Figure 3C) and NREMS fragmentation by MAs (Figure 3D; Franken et al., 1999), were not altered by treatment or time post-surgery (mixed-model ANOVA with factors 'treatment' and 'day,' for sleep onset latency, p=0.42 and p=0.94, no interactions; for number of MAs, p=0.79 and p=0.43, no interactions).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (mixed-model ANOVAs) of microarousal frequency data shown in Figure 3D and cites Franken et al., 1999.

claim: Heart rate was higher in NREMS after SNI at D20+ compared to baseline.
source: We found that heart rate was higher in NREMS after SNI at D20+ compared to baseline (Figure 3E, mixed-model ANOVA with factors 'treatment' × 'state' × 'day' with interaction, p=0.02, post-hoc paired t-test for SNI in NREMS, p = 0.002, with Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.0125).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (mixed-model ANOVA and post-hoc paired t-test) of heart rate data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: SNI raised heart rate, suggesting elevated sympathetic cardiovascular activation in this model of neuropathic pain.
source: SNI thus raised heart rate, suggesting elevated sympathetic cardiovascular activation in this model of neuropathic pain.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the heart rate data and draws on knowledge about the relationship between heart rate and sympathetic activation.

claim: Both NREMS and REMS showed characteristic spectral peaks at delta (1–4 Hz) and at theta frequencies (5–10 Hz), respectively, which were indistinguishable between Sham and SNI groups and from baseline to D20+.
source: Both NREMS and REMS showed the respective characteristic spectral peaks at delta (1–4 Hz) and at theta frequencies (5–10 Hz), respectively. These were indistinguishable between the two groups of animals and from baseline to D20+ (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by power spectral density data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Relative gamma power was increased in SNI at D20+ compared to baseline in NREMS.
source: In contrast to the preserved low-frequency power, relative gamma power was increased in SNI at D20+ compared to baseline in NREMS (Figure 3F, one-sample t-test for NREMS in SNI, p=0.0092).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (one-sample t-test) of gamma power data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: There were no correlations between relative changes in gamma power and alterations in sleep architecture in individual mice.
source: There were no correlations between relative changes in gamma power and alterations in sleep architecture in individual mice (change in the number of MAs per hour of NREMS × change in gamma power; pairwise linear correlation R2 = 0.09, p=0.08; change in total NREMS time × change in gamma power; R2 = 0.02, p = 0.36).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of gamma power and sleep architecture measures.

claim: After SNI mice do not suffer from major alterations in sleep-wake behaviors.
source: These data indicate that after SNI mice do not suffer from major alterations in sleep-wake behaviors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing preserved sleep architecture and spectral properties.

claim: Pathological increases in wake-related brain rhythms and increases in heart rate continued to be present in sleep after SNI.
source: However, pathological increases in wake-related brain rhythms and increases in heart rate continued to be present in sleep.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing increased gamma power in NREMS and elevated heart rate during sleep in SNI animals.

claim: The 0.02 Hz-fluctuation was not different between Sham and SNI across the light phase in terms of amplitude or frequency.
source: The 0.02 Hz-fluctuation was not different between Sham and SNI (n = 18 for both groups) across the light phase. Thus, neither its amplitude nor frequency (Figure 4A–C), or, equivalently, the number of its cycles per hour of NREMS, were different between the groups (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: The phase-coupling of microarousals to the 0.02 Hz-fluctuation was unaltered between Sham and SNI.
source: The phase-coupling to MAs was also unaltered (Figure 4E, mean angle ± 95% confidence interval [CI]: 152.3 ± 1.4 for Sham and 150.4 ± 1.3 for SNI) and the distribution of fragility periods containing transitions to MAs, to REMS, or with continuation into NREMS was indistinguishable (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by phase analysis data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: The distribution of fragility periods containing transitions to microarousals, to REMS, or with continuation into NREMS was indistinguishable between Sham and SNI.
source: The phase-coupling to MAs was also unaltered (Figure 4E, mean angle ± 95% confidence interval [CI]: 152.3 ± 1.4 for Sham and 150.4 ± 1.3 for SNI) and the distribution of fragility periods containing transitions to MAs, to REMS, or with continuation into NREMS was indistinguishable (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Sleep deprivation confirmed a characteristic rebound of delta power in both Sham and SNI groups.
source: We therefore carried out a 6 hr sleep deprivation (SD) at the beginning of the light phase as done previously in the lab (n = 12 for Sham and SNI each) (Kopp et al., 2006). We confirmed a characteristic rebound of delta power (Figure 4G and H) and a decrease in the frequency of MAs (Figure 4I and J, mixed-model ANOVA with factors 'treatment' and 'SD,' p=0.35 and p=1.23 × 10–7 with no interaction).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G and H and cites Kopp et al., 2006.

claim: Sleep deprivation resulted in a decrease in the frequency of microarousals in both Sham and SNI groups.
source: We therefore carried out a 6 hr sleep deprivation (SD) at the beginning of the light phase as done previously in the lab (n = 12 for Sham and SNI each) (Kopp et al., 2006). We confirmed a characteristic rebound of delta power (Figure 4G and H) and a decrease in the frequency of MAs (Figure 4I and J, mixed-model ANOVA with factors 'treatment' and 'SD,' p=0.35 and p=1.23 × 10–7 with no interaction).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (mixed-model ANOVA) of microarousal frequency data shown in Figure 4I and J and cites Kopp et al., 2006.

claim: The phase-coupling of microarousals to the 0.02 Hz-fluctuation remained unaltered in both groups even with high sleep pressure.
source: The phase-coupling of MAs to the 0.02 Hz-fluctuation remained unaltered in both groups even with high sleep pressure (Figure 4K and L).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4K and L.

claim: SNI left spontaneous microarousals, their coupling to the 0.02 Hz-fluctuation, as well as homeostatic regulation of spontaneous arousability unaltered.
source: SNI thus left spontaneous MAs, their coupling to the 0.02 Hz-fluctuation, as well as homeostatic regulation of spontaneous arousability unaltered.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing no differences in microarousal frequency, phase-coupling, or response to sleep deprivation between Sham and SNI groups.

claim: The 0.02 Hz-fluctuation showed a higher peak in S1HL than in PrL.
source: Consistent with its predominant expression in sensory cortices (Lecci et al., 2017), the 0.02 Hz-fluctuation showed a higher peak in S1HL than in PrL (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and B and cites Lecci et al., 2017.

claim: After SNI, mice showed alterations in relative amplitude and dynamics in S1HL, but not in PrL.
source: Analysis across power bands revealed that, after SNI, mice showed alterations in relative amplitude and dynamics in S1HL, but not in PrL.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 5C-J comparing spectral dynamics in S1HL and PrL.

claim: Delta power was lower after SNI during fragility periods in S1HL.
source: In particular, delta power was lower after SNI during fragility periods (Figure 5C, mixed-model ANOVA with factors 'treatment' and 'period,' p=0.001 for the interaction).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (mixed-model ANOVA) of delta power data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In Sham controls there was a distinct rapid upstroke of delta power that reached a peak during the fragility periods.
source: While in Sham controls there was a distinct rapid upstroke of power in this frequency band that reached a peak during the fragility periods (post-hoc t-test for delta power in fragility vs. continuity period in Sham, p=0.001), there was no such elevation detectable in delta power in SNI (post-hoc t-test in SNI, p=0.44).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (post-hoc t-test) of delta power dynamics.

claim: There was no elevation detectable in delta power during fragility periods in SNI.
source: While in Sham controls there was a distinct rapid upstroke of power in this frequency band that reached a peak during the fragility periods (post-hoc t-test for delta power in fragility vs. continuity period in Sham, p=0.001), there was no such elevation detectable in delta power in SNI (post-hoc t-test in SNI, p=0.44).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (post-hoc t-test) of delta power dynamics.

claim: Fragility periods after SNI were destabilized compared to Sham.
source: This difference indicates that fragility periods after SNI were destabilized compared to Sham.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the altered delta power dynamics during fragility periods in SNI.

claim: The high-frequency bands in the beta and low-gamma range showed a tonic increase after SNI that was present throughout continuity and fragility periods in S1HL.
source: Further supporting this, the high-frequency bands in the beta and low-gamma range showed a tonic increase after SNI that was present throughout continuity and fragility periods in S1HL (Figure 5D–F, mixed-model ANOVA with factors 'treatment' and 'period,' for beta, p=0.01, p=1.3 × 10–9 and for low gamma, p=0.005, p=1.4 × 10–10) and that was also present, although to a milder extent, in the high-gamma range (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (mixed-model ANOVAs) of beta and low-gamma power data shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: The tonic increase in high-frequency bands after SNI was also present in the high-gamma range, although to a milder extent.
source: Further supporting this, the high-frequency bands in the beta and low-gamma range showed a tonic increase after SNI that was present throughout continuity and fragility periods in S1HL (Figure 5D–F, mixed-model ANOVA with factors 'treatment' and 'period,' for beta, p=0.01, p=1.3 × 10–9 and for low gamma, p=0.005, p=1.4 × 10–10) and that was also present, although to a milder extent, in the high-gamma range (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The activation index is a measure for the degree of arousal and increases when NREMS moves closer to wakefulness.
source: This AI is a measure for the degree of arousal and increases when NREMS moves closer to wakefulness (Lecci et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Lecci et al., 2020 as the source for this definition.

claim: In the fragility periods continuing into NREMS and being devoid of EMG activity, the activation index decreased, consistent with NREMS remaining consolidated.
source: In the fragility periods continuing into NREMS and being devoid of EMG activity, the AI decreased, consistent with NREMS remaining consolidated (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: After SNI, the mean activation index was higher compared to Sham specifically in the fragility periods.
source: After SNI, however, the mean AI was higher compared to Sham specifically in the fragility periods (Figure 6B, mixed-model ANOVA with factors 'treatment' and 'period,' p=0.039 for interaction, post-hoc t-tests Sham vs. SNI in fragility period, p=0.005, in continuity period, p=0.027, not significant with α = 0.0125).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (mixed-model ANOVA and post-hoc t-tests) of activation index data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Fragility periods during uninterrupted NREMS were moments during which the activation index after SNI was specifically higher compared to continuity periods.
source: Fragility periods during uninterrupted NREMS were thus moments during which the AI after SNI was specifically higher compared to continuity periods.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the activation index data showing higher values during fragility periods in SNI.

claim: The activation index showed an intermittent phasic peak in most microarousals (75.2% ± 4.1%).
source: As expected, the AI showed an intermittent phasic peak (Figure 6D–F) in most MAs (75.2% ± 4.1%), which is explained by the strong decline in delta power (see Figure 1C) and the appearance of higher frequencies associated with MAs.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: A subset of fragility periods continuing into NREMS (without a microarousal) contained an intermittent peak in activation index resembling the one found during microarousals.
source: Therefore, we inspected individual fragility periods continuing into NREMS (without an MA) for the presence of similar phasic increases in AI. Indeed, we noticed that a subset of these did contain an intermittent peak resembling the one found during MAs (Figure 6G) and not evident in the mean AI in Figure 6B.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Heart rate was distinctly higher during the fragility period for cycles containing an activation index peak as opposed to the ones without such peak.
source: The heart rate was distinctly higher during the fragility period for cycles containing an AI peak as opposed to the ones without such peak (Figure 6H, mixed-model ANOVA with factors 'treatment,' 'period,' and 'peak', p=0.007 for the 'peak' × 'period' interaction).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (mixed-model ANOVA) of heart rate data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Fragility periods with activation index peaks were more frequent after SNI and followed a similar time of day dependence as the classical microarousals.
source: Although they are present in both groups, these events were more frequent after SNI and followed a similar time of day dependence as the classical MAs ((Figure 6I and J), t-test Sham vs. SNI, p=0.02).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of the occurrence of fragility periods with activation index peaks shown in Figure 6I and J.

claim: The increased occurrence of fragility periods with activation index peaks was specific for S1HL while absent in PrL and in the contralateral EEG.
source: Moreover, their increased occurrence was specific for S1HL while absent in PrL and in the contralateral EEG (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rodent NREMS shows local cortical intrusion of wake-related activity in the absence of muscular activity.
source: First, it demonstrates that rodent NREMS shows local cortical intrusion of wake-related activity in the absence of muscular activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of activation index peaks during NREMS without EMG activity.

claim: Local cortical arousals in SNI showed intermittent peaks in activation index that were close to the ones of microarousals, indicating comparable cortical desynchronization at the local level.
source: Second, these local cortical arousals in SNI showed intermittent peaks in AI that were close to the ones of MAs, indicating comparable cortical desynchronization at the local level.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of activation index peaks in fragility periods and microarousals.

claim: Local cortical arousals were accompanied by heart rate increases that are sensitive hallmarks of arousal in human.
source: Third, they were accompanied by heart rate increases that are sensitive hallmarks of arousal in human (Azarbarzin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by heart rate data and cites Azarbarzin et al., 2014.

claim: Nerve injury increased the relative occurrence of fragility periods with activation index peaks specifically in the S1HL area.
source: Fourth, nerve injury increased the relative occurrence of fragility periods with such AI peaks specifically in the S1HL area.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing increased occurrence of these events in S1HL but not in PrL or contralateral EEG.

claim: The machine learning software was trained to predict online periods of continuity and fragility based on EEG/EMG recordings.
source: To anticipate fragility and continuity periods in real time in the sleeping animal, we trained a machine learning software to predict online periods of continuity and fragility based on EEG/EMG recordings (Figure 7A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the machine learning approach shown in Figure 7A-E.

claim: The microarousal proportions obtained with the real online detection exceeded those obtained by chance prediction.
source: We compared the online prediction to that generated by chance through randomly shuffling both online fragility and continuity point positions in the recordings. This showed that the MA proportions obtained with the real detection exceeded those obtained by chance prediction (Figure 7G, for online fragility periods, p=0.0004, for online continuity periods, p=0.0028).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of real vs. chance detection shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Online detection of peak-to-trough and trough-to-peak periods of the 0.02 Hz-fluctuation is a versatile method to probe variations of evoked arousability from NREMS.
source: Online detection of peak-to-trough and trough-to-peak periods of the 0.02 Hz-fluctuation is thus a versatile method to probe variations of evoked arousability from NREMS.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the successful validation of the online detection method.

claim: After SNI, sensory arousability was elevated for both continuity and fragility periods.
source: After SNI, sensory arousability was elevated for both continuity and fragility periods, leading to highest values during the online fragility periods (Figure 8D, mixed-model ANOVA with factors 'treatment' and 'online period,' p=0.0049 for 'treatment,' p=1.31 × 10–8 for 'online period,' no interaction).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (mixed-model ANOVA) of wake-up probability data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The increase in sensory arousability after SNI was present across the whole light phase with a conserved time of day dependence.
source: Interestingly, consistent with the tonic increase in AI, this increase in sensory arousability after SNI was present across the whole light phase with a conserved time of day dependence (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Infraslow fluctuations in brain excitability and connectivity could render the sleeping brain vulnerable to spontaneous disruptive events, including more frequent arousals in case of sleep disorders.
source: Infraslow fluctuations in brain excitability and connectivity could render the sleeping brain vulnerable to spontaneous disruptive events, including more frequent arousals in case of sleep disorders.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on the observed relationship between infraslow fluctuations and arousal occurrence.

claim: Experimental models of peripheral neuropathic pain rely on surgically crushing or lesioning peripheral nerves, such as the sciatic nerve.
source: Experimental models of peripheral neuropathic pain rely on surgically crushing or lesioning peripheral nerves, such as the sciatic nerve (Jaggi et al., 2011; Challa, 2015).
evidence: The claim cites Jaggi et al., 2011 and Challa, 2015 as sources for this information.

claim: These models have allowed numerous breakthrough understandings on chronic pain mechanisms.
source: In spite of their limitations, these models have allowed numerous breakthrough understandings on chronic pain mechanisms (Kuner and Kuner, 2020) and avenues for treatment (Finnerup et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Kuner and Kuner, 2020 as the source for this information.

claim: Sleep studies on chronic pain models are scarce and have produced variable results.
source: In contrast, sleep studies on chronic pain models are scarce and have produced variable results (Andersen and Tufik, 2003; Kontinen et al., 2003; Tokunaga et al., 2007; Cardoso-Cruz et al., 2011; Leys et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim cites multiple studies (Andersen and Tufik, 2003; Kontinen et al., 2003; Tokunaga et al., 2007; Cardoso-Cruz et al., 2011; Leys et al., 2013) as sources for this information.

claim: When mouse NREMS is vulnerable to sensory stimuli, it is also vulnerable to spontaneous arousals.
source: Therefore, when mouse NREMS is vulnerable to sensory stimuli, it is also vulnerable to spontaneous arousals.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both sensory arousals and microarousals occur preferentially during fragility periods.

claim: Sensory arousals and microarousals may have common mechanistic origins.
source: Sensory arousals and MAs may have common mechanistic origins, in line with evidence that both depend on activity in wake-promoting brain areas (Léna et al., 2004; Huang et al., 2006; Dvir et al., 2018; Mátyás et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is speculative and cites multiple studies (Léna et al., 2004; Huang et al., 2006; Dvir et al., 2018; Mátyás et al., 2018) as supporting evidence.

claim: Infraslow time scales determine the vulnerability of NREMS for both weak (in case of spontaneous arousals) and more intense (in case of evoked arousals) levels of wake-promoting input.
source: Furthermore, the result suggests that infraslow time scales determine the vulnerability of NREMS for both weak (in case of spontaneous arousals) and more intense (in case of evoked arousals) levels of wake-promoting input.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both spontaneous and evoked arousals are related to the infraslow fluctuation.

claim: The increased delta power and decreased activation index in S1HL in fragility periods continuing into NREMS signal momentarily increased sleep depth.
source: The increased delta power and decreased AI in S1HL in fragility periods continuing into NREMS seem at odds with this finding because they signal momentarily increased sleep depth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the interpretation of delta power and activation index as measures of sleep depth.

claim: These dynamics are likely a consequence of an incompatibility between sigma and delta power in sensory thalamocortical loops.
source: These dynamics are likely a consequence of an incompatibility between sigma and delta power in sensory thalamocortical loops (Fernandez et al., 2018) that are not, however, strong enough to override the vulnerability of NREMS identified here.
evidence: The claim is speculative and cites Fernandez et al., 2018 as supporting evidence.

claim: Heart rate increases occur even for very weak cortical arousals in human NREMS.
source: It also concurs with human NREMS in which heart rate increases occur even for very weak cortical arousals (Azarbarzin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim cites Azarbarzin et al., 2014 as the source for this information.

claim: The cortical regions in which arousals appeared coincided with sites known to be affected by neuropathic pain.
source: We found that the cortical regions in which arousals appeared coincided with sites known to be affected by neuropathic pain.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of increased arousals in S1HL, a pain-processing area.

claim: The continued presence of high-frequency activity in S1HL is reminiscent of the cortical oscillatory activity present during withdrawal from acute painful stimuli.
source: The continued presence of high-frequency activity in S1HL is reminiscent of the cortical oscillatory activity present during withdrawal from acute painful stimuli (Tan et al., 2019), suggesting that, after SNI, nociceptive input continues to arrive in cortex during NREMS to generate excessive excitation.
evidence: The claim cites Tan et al., 2019 and is speculative about the mechanism.

claim: It has been suggested that the SNI model does show spontaneous ectopic electrical activity in peripheral sensory neurons as a result of nerve injury that can increase nociceptive inputs.
source: Indeed, it has been suggested that the SNI model does show spontaneous ectopic electrical activity in peripheral sensory neurons as a result of nerve injury that can increase nociceptive inputs (Wall and Devor, 1983; Devor, 2009).
evidence: The claim cites Wall and Devor, 1983 and Devor, 2009 as sources for this information.

claim: NREMS is thought to protect relatively weakly from nociceptive inputs.
source: NREMS is thought to protect relatively weakly from nociceptive inputs (Claude et al., 2015), therefore possibly allowing continued processing of spontaneous nociceptive activity that could explain the cortical spectral changes we detected.
evidence: The claim cites Claude et al., 2015 as the source for this information.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) alleviates SNI-related pain.
source: We mention that optogenetic stimulation of the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) alleviates SNI-related pain (LeBlanc et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim cites LeBlanc et al., 2017 as the source for this information.

claim: TRN is involved in the regulation of low-frequency power during NREMS.
source: As TRN is involved in the regulation of low-frequency power during NREMS (Fernandez et al., 2018), the attenuated delta dynamics observed in NREMS after SNI could result also from altered activity in this nucleus.
evidence: The claim cites Fernandez et al., 2018 and is speculative about the mechanism.

claim: The animals were analyzed at a time point when pain from the incision and associated inflammations are largely over.
source: First, we analyzed these animals at a time point when pain from the incision and associated inflammations are largely over (Guida et al., 2020), both of which have been shown to disrupt sleep (Landis et al., 1989; Silva et al., 2008; Leys et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim cites Guida et al., 2020, Landis et al., 1989, Silva et al., 2008, and Leys et al., 2013 as sources for this information.

claim: The animals showed a preserved time spent in REMS, suggesting that they did not suffer from chronic mild stress-inflicted sleep disruptions.
source: Moreover, the animals showed a preserved time spent in REMS, suggesting that they did not suffer from chronic mild stress-inflicted sleep disruptions (Nollet et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the REMS data and cites Nollet et al., 2019.

claim: Patients with insomnia show imbalances in the contribution of low vs. higher frequencies over widespread brain regions that include sensorimotor areas.
source: Patients with insomnia show such imbalances over widespread brain regions that include sensorimotor areas (Lecci et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Lecci et al., 2020 as the source for this information.

claim: Higher power in the beta frequencies has been related to patients remaining hypervigilant or excessively ruminating at sleep onset.
source: Furthermore, higher power in the beta frequencies has been related to the patients remaining hypervigilant or excessively ruminating at sleep onset (Perlis et al., 2001), preventing the deactivation of cortical processes required for the loss of consciousness.
evidence: The claim cites Perlis et al., 2001 as the source for this information.

claim: Deficits in working and declarative memories in rodents with SNI have been documented from early periods of chronic pain.
source: Deficits in working and declarative memories in rodents with SNI have been documented from early periods of chronic pain (Guida et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Guida et al., 2020 as the source for this information.

claim: SNI in mouse qualifies as a rodent model replicating physiological correlates of sleep disorders that are hidden behind a comparatively normal sleep architecture.
source: SNI in mouse qualifies as a rodent model replicating physiological correlates of sleep disorders that are hidden behind a comparatively normal sleep architecture, which is of interest in the field of insomnia (Lecci et al., 2020; van Someren, 2020).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the findings and cites Lecci et al., 2020 and van Someren, 2020.

claim: The location of these arousals within the primary cortical sights of pain makes it obvious that the cortical pain axis is causal to sleep disruptions.
source: The location of these arousals within the primary cortical sights of pain makes it obvious that the cortical pain axis is causal to sleep disruptions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of increased arousals in pain-processing cortical areas.

claim: Non-invasive brain stimulation techniques applied locally over sensory or motor cortices have been proposed as therapeutic strategy.
source: Non-invasive brain stimulation techniques applied locally over sensory or motor cortices have been proposed as therapeutic strategy (Lefaucheur et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Lefaucheur et al., 2020 as the source for this information.

claim: More frequent awakenings are amongst the most consistent effects reported in chronic pain patients.
source: The insights gained from this rodent model of neuropathic pain could thus refine diagnosis and management strategies in the human condition, in which more frequent awakenings are amongst the most consistent effects reported.
evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge about sleep disruptions in chronic pain patients.
